Each of the individual course changes as well as this overall program change reflects significant student-focused alterations that strategically and systemically support our adult-learner student population. Included with these documents are our Professional Leadership Studies Curriculum Sheet (track-changed) that indicate the positive impact it will have for our students. Ultimately, we will be providing them with (a) a cohort-style experience with other adult learners, (b) flexibility to craft a learning experience that capitalizes on their professional growth, and (c) courses that offer knowledge-acquisition and skills-development that resonate with the needs of professional workplaces. In summation, the Professional Leadership Studies program changes include: • SPC 211 (Professional Communication) o A new course designed to enhance the professional writing and communication of our Professional Studies students. • SPC 221 (Finance and Budgeting for Professional Workplaces) o A shift in course number a title to entice students from across Professional Studies to take it earlier in their academic journey.

2 • SPC 325 (Socially-Just and Culturally-Relevant Leadership for the Workplace) o A new course that prepares students to effectively lead diverse organizations with a social justice and equity lens. • SPC 335 (Planning and Analysis)—formally SPC 207 o A shift in course number to make it a more advanced course and hopefully attract non-Professional Studies to take it as a 300-level elective. • SPC 490 (Independent Study) o A new course to give both students and faculty an opportunity to craft independent courses that resonate with innovative learning experiences.
For students, they will be able to propose courses not traditionally offered that might propel their growth for work and community engagements, create opportunities for a research project, or explore a specialized interest in professional studies in a deeper, more meaningful way. • SPC 495 (Special Topics) o A new course that provides faculty an outlet to be responsive to learning opportunities that go beyond the traditional curriculum.
The “Special Topics” seminar is devised to be utilized for courses that address contemporary topics, problems, and issues that our professional workplaces face.

Additionally, course this will enable us to craft new learning experiences in international contexts (e.g., “Comparative Leadership: Taiwan and the USA” or “International NGO and Social Sector Impact in the Dominican Republic”) that are not traditionally offered within the curriculum.
Overall, these changes will install a cohort-style experience by encouraging students from across Professional Studies to take three 200-level courses (i.e., SPC 201, 211, and 221) together at the start of the academic journey.
Similarly, they will take SPC 499 as a Professional Studies-wide culminating educational experience.
These four courses are intended to be required for the Professional Leadership Studies degree.
Students will then have the option of taking other PLS-approved SPC courses to secure their remaining eighteen major credits.
This may include the traditional courses (SPC 215, 325, 335, 401, 420, 450), an internship experience for up to six credits (SPC 480), or an Independent Study / Special Topics for up to six credits (SPC 490, 495). 6.

Explain why the organizational change is being proposed.

Film/Media has long functioned as a department, without being awarded Departmental status.
FLM operates as a fully-fledged university department and is expected to fulfill the demands, expectations, and duties of an academic unit at that level: Film/Media has its own budget--and in addition to the budget afforded to us from the College of Arts & Sciences and the University, we manage approximately $125,000 in lab fees annually which are used to purchase and repair equipment, hardware and software, and to meet the financial demands that are necessary to adequately deliver courses and classrooms for the major.
Film/Media’s director fulfills all of the obligations and responsibilities of a department chair, and our faculty--tenure-track, full-time, Joint, and PTF--who exemplify dedicated and engaged pedagogical and scholarly rigor-- do not benefit from being identified or recognized as members of a valued academic department and discipline in the University.

Film/Media recorded 236 majors in Oct. 2020 and is the 5th largest major in Arts & Sciences, and the 2nd largest in the Harrington School.
The major has grown by 43% in the 5 years since 2017.
The program has served as a flagship for the Harrington School and the University in attracting prospective students, and, for the most part, the number of our incoming Freshmen class has grown steadily over the years from 28 in AY 2007 to an entering class of 48 in September 2020.
It should be noted that in the four B.A.-granting undergraduate majors that comprise the Harrington School, all except FLM operate with departmental status, although FLM is larger than two of the other three in the number of our majors, our budget, and the number of incoming freshmen that we attract each year.
The Department of Writing and Rhetoric has 42 majors, while the Department of Journalism has 88 majors [data for Fall 2021 semester].

Film/Media, serving 224 majors this Fall, is not given parity with these other units, which presents an unclear, confusing, and lopsided picture of the emphasis, resource allocation, and focus of the Harrington School and its aims, goals and the importance of its students within the overall structure.
This inequity sends a message to prospective and current students and their families that Film/Media may be less important and less vital than the rest of the Harrington School, and that it might not be the recipient of the attention and resources that a future major might desire.

FLM has historically had to function with an extremely small faculty (1.5 tenure-track and 3 full-time Lecturers--the most recent only hired in 2020) and has been granted a TT line only once in its history, in 2010.
The lack of departmental status has certainly contributed to the University’s lack of investment in our major, creating a cycle that only allows growth to a certain point before it becomes unsustainable.
Film/Media’s student: teacher ratio was 22.6 in 2019 [CDR] with only 3% of credit hours delivered by tenure-track faculty.
